newsitem.title: FRANCE: Club Med reports loss, Triganos walk out.
newsitem.headline: Club Med reports loss, Triganos walk out.

text.p: The founders of Club Med quit Friday in a dispute over the direction of the French resort chain, which reported a big loss for the first half of its fiscal year.
Serge Trigano said that he and his father Gilbert, who co-founded the firm in 1950, had resigned from the supervisory board after a dispute with Philippe Bourguignon, who heads the management board.
Bourguignon took over from Serge Trigano in February after rescuing Euro Disney and turning Mickey Mouse's Paris outpost into Europe's top tourist attraction.
Club Mediterranee said it lost $68 million in the six months ended on April 30, largely because of a $104 million restructuring charge, and said it may take more charges later this year.
Bourguignon said he wanted to revitalise the company that pioneered all-inclusive, fun-in-the-sun holidays but preserve its culture and concept.
But Trigano told Europe 1 radio that the company's chic holiday villages risked turning into "Mickey (Mouse) clubs" and it was time for the founders to get out.

"There was a certain spirit in this firm, a certain soul based on love, tenderness and generosity. I don't know if it will be a Mickey Club or something else but it will certainly be a different club from the past," he said.
"The new team has its own methods which are not mine and there is no place left for a Trigano."
He suggested that the Trigano family planned to launch a rival holiday club chain, addressing a different audience such as older people.
Club Med, synonymous with holiday villages for three generations of European tourists, took a $135 million restructuring charge last year and lost about $123 million.
It posted operating profits of about $14 million in the first half ended in April but that was wiped out by interest payments and the charge.
Investors welcomed Bourguignon's approach, and the company's stock jumped nearly 6 percent to 445 francs ($73.50) in Paris.

"The Triganos focused on the product. Bourguignon sees that it's a good product, but poorly sold," said analyst Antoine Nodet at French brokerage Natexis. He and several other brokers raised their ratings on the stock to outperform.

"The Club has fantastic potential which is under-exploited today due to multiple weaknesses," Bourguignon said in a letter to shareholders. "Club Med is a great brand. It needs to preserve its culture but change its operating methods."
After cleaning up the balance sheet this year, Club Med will strive to lure back customers with attractive prices. It plans to step up new resort openings in 2000.
"This is a company that is growing, not one that's selling cruise ships, closing vacation villages," Bourguignon said, chiding the Triganos' past retrenchment moves.
Club Med said sales rose 2 percent to $644 million from $629 million, largely due to a stronger dollar and higher prices prices that offset sluggish demand.
Despite the loss, its financial situation remains "healthy" with debt of $396 million and $578 million in shareholder equity, it said.
